notes.15:18: The Greek explicitly names 'David' as his father and reads 'the holy things of the house of the Lord God' (rather than 'his own dedicated things into the house of God' as in the Hebrew).
notes.16:1: The Greek dates Baasha's invasion to the 'thirty-eighth year' of Asa's reign, whereas the Hebrew text reads the 'thirty-sixth year.'
notes.16:2: The Greek renders the Hebrew royal name Ben-hadad literally as 'the son of Hader' (also in v. 4), with the variant spelling Hader, and in v. 3 reads 'scatter Baasha' without mentioning a broken treaty.
notes.16:4: The Greek preserves the distinct town names 'Io,' 'Dano,' and 'Abelman' (corresponding to Hebrew Ijon, Dan, and Abel-maim) and reads 'all the surrounding districts of Naphtali' rather than 'all the store cities.'
notes.16:7: The Greek gives the prophet's name as 'Hanami' (where the Hebrew has 'Hanani the seer'), and in v. 8 reads 'with boldness' (Greek tharsos) where the Hebrew has 'with chariots.'
notes.16:9: The Greek phrase rendered 'concerning what is toward Him' (epi tou pros auton) is syntactically difficult and could alternatively be taken as 'upon the one who is toward Him.'
notes.16:13: The Greek states that Asa died in the 'thirtieth year' of his reign (despite the 'thirty-ninth year' in v. 12; the Hebrew has 'forty-first year'), and in v. 14 reads 'a very great funeral' (Greek ekphoran) rather than a great fire.
notes.17:3: Greek reads simply "his father" (i.e., Asa), omitting "David," and renders Hebrew "the Baals" as "the idols"; in v. 4 Greek similarly reads "the commandments of his father" where MT has "His commandments."
notes.17:7: Greek translates the Hebrew proper name Ben-hail literally as "the sons of the mighty men" and reads "Abijah" (Abias) where MT has Obadiah.
notes.17:8: Several names differ from MT: Greek has Samuas (MT Shemaiah), Manthanias (MT Nethaniah), Jasiel (MT Asahel), and a single name Tobadobiah (MT Tobijah and Tob-adonijah).
notes.17:11: Greek "foreigners" (allophyloi) is the Septuagint's standard designation for the Philistines; Greek also lists only seven thousand seven hundred rams of sheep, omitting the seven thousand seven hundred male goats found in MT.
notes.17:16: Greek reads "Masaias son of Zari" where MT has Amasiah son of Zichri.
notes.18:7: Greek reads "Jemaa" (Iemaas here and Iemaa in v. 8) where MT has Imlah.
notes.18:10: Greek reads "Canaan" (Chanaan, also in v. 23) where MT has Chenaanah.
notes.18:18: Greek opens Micaiah's speech with "Not so!" (reading the Hebrew consonants as lo ken) where MT has "Therefore" (laken).
notes.18:23: The Greek text lacks a verb and repeats "spirit" (pneuma) three times in an apparent textual conflation (contrast MT "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?").
notes.18:25: Greek reads "Emer" where MT has Amon, and adds "the ruler" before "son of the king"; in v. 24 Greek also reads third-person singular "he will enter" where MT has second-person "when you go."
notes.18:29: Greek reads the imperative "Disguise me" and "my clothing," whereas MT has "I will disguise myself" and "your robes."
notes.18:33: Greek reads "with sure aim" (eustochos) where MT has "at random," and "the lung" (tou pneumonos) where MT has "the joints/scale-armor."
notes.19:2: Greek reads passive "one hated by the Lord" where MT has active "those who hate the LORD," and places "King Jehoshaphat" as a direct vocative opening Jehu's speech.
notes.19:6: Greek has nominative plural "the matters of judgment" (logoi tes kriseos) as the subject ("with you are the matters of judgment"), whereas MT reads "He is with you in the matter of judgment."
notes.19:8: Greek reads "to judge those who dwell in Jerusalem," reading the Hebrew consonants as "inhabitants" rather than MT's "and they returned to Jerusalem."
notes.19:10: The Greek syntax is compressed and broken, reading "every man" alongside "the case," "our brothers" (MT "your brothers"), and a single "blood" without "in their cities."
notes.20:1: The Greek text reads "Meunites" (Meinaiōn), whereas the Hebrew text reads "Ammonites."
notes.20:2: The Greek text reads "Hasam Thamara," whereas the Hebrew text reads "Hazazon-tamar."
notes.20:14: The Greek genealogy reads "Oziel, the son of Zechariah, of the sons of Eleael, the son of Manthanias," whereas the Hebrew text reads "Jahaziel son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah."
notes.20:16: The Greek text reads "Hasae" and "Jeriel," whereas the Hebrew text reads "Ziz" and "Jeruel."
notes.20:17: The Greek text reads "understand these things," "Look, also Jerusalem," and "be afraid of him" (auton), whereas the Hebrew text reads "position yourselves, stand," "Judah and Jerusalem," and "tomorrow" (reflecting an inner-Greek shift from aurion to auton).
notes.20:34: The Greek text reads "Joshua" (Iēsou) and "who wrote the book of the king of Israel," whereas the Hebrew text reads "Jehu" and "which were recorded in the book of the kings of Israel."
notes.20:37: The Greek text reads "Eliada the son of Odeia," whereas the Hebrew text reads "Eliezer son of Dodavahu."
notes.21:2: Although the Greek text states "six" brothers, it names only four (omitting the two named Azariah in the Hebrew text) and reads "Mishael" (Meisaēl) where the Hebrew text reads "Michael."
notes.21:16: Greek allophylous ("foreigners") is the Septuagint's standard rendering for "Philistines."
notes.21:17: The Greek text reads "his daughters," whereas the Hebrew text reads "his wives."
notes.21:19: The Greek text literally reads "two days" (hēmeras dyo, rendering the Hebrew idiom for "two years") and "funeral" (ekphoran, where the Hebrew text reads "burning").
notes.22:1: The Greek text adds "the Alimazonites" (hoi Aleimazoneis) after "the Arabs," which does not appear in the Hebrew text.
notes.22:2: The Greek text reads "twenty years old," whereas the Hebrew text reads "forty-two years old" (compare "twenty-two" in 2 Kings 8:26).
notes.22:5: The Greek text reads "the archers" (hoi toxotai), whereas the Hebrew text reads "the Syrians" (Arameans).
notes.22:6: The Greek text twice reads "Israel," whereas the Hebrew text reads "Jezreel."
notes.22:7: The Greek text omits the name "Jehu" before "the son of Nimshi" and omits a verb (such as "to cut off" in the Hebrew text) before the closing phrase "the house of Ahab."
notes.22:9: The Greek text reads "while he was being healed" (iatreuomenon), whereas the Hebrew text reads "while he was hiding himself."
notes.23:1: The Greek text reads "the eighth year" (MT "seventh"), lists "Aziah" and "Elishaphan son of Zechariah" (MT "Adaiah" and "Elishaphat son of Zichri"), and has "into a house" (likely reading Hebrew bbyt instead of bbryt, "into a covenant").
notes.23:5: The Greek text reads "the middle gate," whereas the Hebrew MT has "the Gate of the Foundation."
notes.23:13: Greek epitithemenoi epitithesthe (lit. "conspiring, you conspire") renders Athaliah's outcry as an emphatic accusation of conspiracy (MT "Treason! Treason!").
notes.23:14: The Greek text instructs the commanders to drive Athaliah outside the house, go in after her, and put her to death, whereas the Hebrew MT orders the death of anyone who follows her.
notes.23:20: The Greek text names "the patriarchs" (MT "commanders of hundreds"), says they "brought the king up into the house of the Lord" (MT "down from the house of the Lord"), and specifies "the inner gate" (MT "the upper gate").
notes.24:1: The Greek text gives the queen mother's name as "Abiah," whereas the Hebrew MT reads "Zibiah."
notes.24:5: The Greek text reads "hasten to speak" (MT "hasten the matter") and "the Levites did not believe" (episteusan, likely an inner-Greek variant for espeusan, "did not hasten," matching MT).
notes.24:18: The Greek text reads "the Astartes" (MT "the Asherim") and "on that day" (MT "for this guilt of theirs").
notes.24:20: The Greek text names the priest's son "Azariah," whereas the Hebrew MT reads "Zechariah."
notes.24:26: The Greek text gives the conspirators' names and patronymics as "Zabel the son of Sama the Ammonite" and "Zozabed the son of Somaioth the Moabite," using masculine forms throughout (MT "Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonitess" and "Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabitess").
notes.24:27: Continuing the sentence from verse 26, the Greek text reads "and all his sons, and the five came to him" (apparently reading Hebrew hammas'a, "the oracle/burden," as a word for "five") and omits the MT clause about rebuilding the house of God.
notes.25:1: "Jonaa" renders Greek Ionaa, differing from Hebrew Jehoaddan.
notes.25:17: The Greek text ends concisely after "took counsel," lacking the longer clause in Hebrew where Amaziah sends a challenge to Joash king of Israel.
notes.25:18: "Chozei" and "achouch" are untranslated Greek transliterations of the Hebrew term for "thistle" or "thornbush." The Greek also doubles the clause about the wild beasts, first in the future and then in the past tense.
notes.25:24: "Jabdedom" renders Greek Iabdedom (corresponding to Hebrew Obed-edom), and "sons of the mixtures" reflects Greek symmixeis ("mixtures"), translating the Hebrew term for "hostages." As in Hebrew, an explicit verb ("took") is omitted.
notes.25:25: The Greek text reads "Joash the son of Joash, king of Israel," whereas Hebrew has "Joash the son of Jehoahaz."
notes.26:1: The Greek text reads Ochozeias ("Ahaziah") here before referring to the king as Ozeias ("Uzziah") in verse 3 and throughout the rest of the chapter.
notes.26:3: "Chaaia" renders Greek Chaaia, differing from Hebrew Jecoliah.
notes.26:6: "Foreigners" translates Greek allophyloi, the Septuagint's regular designation for the Philistines. "Abenner" renders Greek Abenner, where Hebrew has Jabneh.
notes.26:11: "Amasaiah" renders Greek Amasaiou (where Hebrew has Maaseiah), and "deputy" reflects Hellenistic court usage of Greek diadochos (literally "successor").
notes.26:21: "Apphousion" is an untranslated Greek transliteration of the Hebrew term for a separate or isolated house. Greek also reads "over his kingdom" where Hebrew has "over the king's house."
notes.26:22: "Jesseiah" renders Greek Iesseiou, a distinct form corresponding to Hebrew "Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz" (with "son of Amoz" absent in Greek).
notes.27:1: "Sador" renders Greek Sador, differing from Hebrew Zadok.
notes.27:3: "Opla" renders Greek Opla (preceded by "its" or "his"), corresponding to Hebrew Ophel.
notes.27:4: The Greek text continues directly from verse 3 without the Hebrew clause "and he built cities," and reads "dwellings" (oikeseis) where Hebrew has "fortresses."
notes.27:9: Verse 27:8, which in Hebrew repeats Jotham's age and reign length from verse 1, is absent from this Greek text.
notes.28:3: Gaibenthom is the Greek transliteration of Hebrew Ge Ben-hinnom ("Valley of the Son of Hinnom"). The Greek also reads "and the abominations" (kai ta bdelygmata), likely an inner-Greek shift from "according to the abominations" (kata ta bdelygmata).
notes.28:5: The Greek reads plural "kings" of Syria and Israel (without mentioning Damascus) and has a reflexive pronoun in the final clause ("struck himself with a great blow").
notes.28:6: The Greek reads "sent" (apesteilen) rather than "killed" (apekteinen), an early Greek scribal variation.
notes.28:10: The Greek closing question literally asks whether it is not for them "with yourselves to bear witness to the Lord our God," diverging from the Hebrew text's reference to "guilts against the LORD your God."
notes.28:12: The Greek names Udeia, Zechariah, Amasiah, and Choad differ from the Hebrew text's Azariah, Berechiah, Amasa, and Hadlai.
notes.28:18: "The foreigners" translates hoi allophyloi, the standard Septuagint designation for the Philistines; the Greek also has the distinct town names Galero and Galezo (corresponding to Gederoth and Gimzo) and omits Timnah.
notes.29:1: The Greek gives the king's mother's name as Abba (compared with Abijah in the Hebrew text and Abi in 2 Kings 18:2).
notes.29:10: The Greek attaches "my" to "covenant" rather than "heart" and uses a past indicative verb ("He has turned away") rather than a wish or purpose clause.
notes.29:12: The Greek Levite list here and in verses 13-14 differs in several names and relationships from the Hebrew text, including Masi (Amasai), Zechariah twice (Azariah), Helle (Jehallelel), Jodan (Eden), Zimri (Shimri), Asa (Asaph), and Azariah (Zechariah).
notes.29:17: The Greek dates the start of the purification to "the third day, the new moon of the first month" and its completion to "the thirteenth day" (compared with the first and sixteenth days in the Hebrew text).
notes.29:35: "The completion of the peace offering" reflects a Greek doublet (tes teleioseos tou soteriou) translating the Hebrew term for peace offerings (shelamim).
notes.30:6: The Greek uses a second-person plural imperative with a direct object ("and bring back those who have been rescued") rather than the Hebrew third-person verb ("and he will return to the remnant"), and reads "God" without "Lord" and singular "king of Assyria."
notes.30:9: The Greek preposition ἀντί ("instead of") here functions like ἔναντι ("before"), and the clause shifts grammatical person ("our God," "from you," "if we return"), with third-person singular future ἀποστρέψει ("He will bring [them] back").
notes.30:14: "To the false ones" (τοῖς ψευδέσιν) is a distinctive Greek expression referring to false gods or idols, not present in the Hebrew text.
notes.30:22: The Greek reads "completed the Feast of Unleavened Bread" where the Hebrew reads "ate the festival," and "sacrifices of deliverance" literally translates θυσίας σωτηρίου, the Septuagint equivalent for peace offerings.
notes.30:24: The Greek reads dative "to Judah" (τῷ Ἰούδᾳ) without "king," and closes with the verbless phrase "and the holy things of the priests in abundance" (τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἱερέων εἰς πλῆθος) where the Hebrew states that priests consecrated themselves in great numbers.
notes.31:6: The Greek reads "tithes of goats" (ἐπιδέκατα αἰγῶν) where the Hebrew reads "tithes of dedicated things," and places "the sons of Israel and Judah" at the end of v. 5 rather than at the start of v. 6.
notes.31:10: The Greek reads "and drunk" (καὶ ἐπίομεν) where the Hebrew reads "and had plenty," and ends with a first-person plural active verb ("we have left over up to this abundance").
notes.31:12: The Greek spells this Levite's name Chomenias (Χωμενίας) here, whereas v. 13 uses the form Conaniah (Χωνενίου) for the same overseer.
notes.31:13: Several names in the Greek differ from the Hebrew list: Eiel (Jehiel), Uzziah (Azaziah), Mahath (Nahath), Ezabath (Jozabad), Jeiel (Eliel), Samachiah (Ismachiah), and Thanai (Mahath); the Greek also adds "and his sons" after Benaiah.
notes.31:15: The Greek reads Heman in v. 14 (Hebrew Imnah) and here lists Odom (Eden), Benjamin (Miniamin), Shimei (Shemaiah), and Marias (Amariah), as well as "by the hand of the priests" where the Hebrew reads "in the cities of the priests."
notes.32:3: The Greek verb is singular ("he supported him"), whereas the context of the elders and mighty men and the Hebrew text suggest the plural ("they supported him").
notes.32:18: The Greek reads "to help them and to pull down" (βοηθῆσαι αὐτοῖς καὶ κατασπάσαι), likely an early Greek textual corruption of φοβῆσαι ("to frighten"), where the Hebrew reads "to frighten them and terrify them."
notes.32:30: The Greek reads "Zion" (Σειών) where the Hebrew reads "Gihon" (compare 33:14, where the Greek has "Gihon").
notes.33:6: "Ge-bene-Hinnom" preserves the Greek transliteration (γὲ βανὲ Ἑννόμ) of the Hebrew phrase meaning "the valley of the sons of Hinnom."
notes.33:14: The Greek renders this passage distinctively as "as one goes out through the surrounding gate" (omitting "Fish" from the Fish Gate) and transcribes Ophel as "Opla" (Ὄπλα).
notes.33:17: The Greek omits "sacrificing" and places "the Lord their God" in the nominative case ("yet the Lord was their God") rather than the dative ("only to the Lord their God").
notes.33:19: The Greek links 33:18 directly to "the words of his prayer, and He heard him" (omitting the reference to the chronicles of the kings of Israel found in the Hebrew) and reads "the seers" where the Hebrew reads "Hozai."
notes.33:20: Here and throughout vv. 20-25, the Greek calls Manasseh's son "Amos" (Ἀμώς) rather than the Hebrew "Amon."
notes.34:8: The Greek names Selia, Maasa, and Juach son of Joah differ from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's Azaliah, Maaseiah, and Joah son of Joahaz.
notes.34:12: The Greek reads the proper name Ie where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has Jahath.
notes.34:17: The Greek verb literally means "melted down" (corresponding to a Hebrew verb meaning "poured out" or "emptied out") and shifts to the singular "he gave it" where the Hebrew has plural "they gave it".
notes.34:20: The Greek names Abdodom and Isaiah correspond to Abdon and Asaiah in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.34:22: The Greek gives Shallum's ancestors as Kathual and Chelles (Hebrew: Tokhath and Hasrah), describes Huldah as "who kept the commandments" (Hebrew: Shallum, "keeper of the wardrobe"), and transliterates Hebrew "the Second Quarter" as a place name, Maasanai.
notes.35:3: The Greek differs markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, describing the Levites as "capable" (Hebrew: "who taught"), turning "who were holy" into an indirect command "to consecrate themselves", and rendering "Put the holy ark" as a completed action, "and they placed the holy ark".
notes.35:9: The Greek includes Benaiah (absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text) and reads Joel where the Hebrew has Jeiel.
notes.35:12: The Greek "until the morning" reflects reading the unvocalized Hebrew consonants for "cattle" as "morning"; similarly in v. 13, "and it went well" reflects reading the Hebrew word for "pans" as a verb meaning "prospered".
notes.35:19: Following the opening temporal phrase, the Greek preserves a lengthy addition parallel to 2 Kings 23:24-27 that is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text of 2 Chronicles. Within this addition, "karaseim" is an untranslated Greek transliteration (corresponding to "abominations" in 2 Kings 23:24), and "statutes" corresponds to "provocations" in 2 Kings 23:26.
notes.35:25: The Greek reads "male and female rulers" where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "singing men and singing women" (from similar-looking Hebrew consonants); in v. 26, "his hope" likewise reflects an alternative reading of the Hebrew for "his loyal deeds".
notes.36:2: The Greek expands this verse with material parallel to 2 Kings 23:31-33 and preserves the distinct names Abital (versus Hamutal in 2 Kings 23:31 MT) and Dablatha (versus Riblah in 2 Kings 23:33 MT).
notes.36:5: The Greek includes a long expansion parallel to 2 Kings 23:36-24:4 with distinct names (Zechora daughter of Neriah from Ramah, and Samaria among the raiders), attributes the innocent blood to Jehoiakim, and reads "not willing to destroy them" rather than "forgive."
notes.36:8: The burial notice is a Greek expansion in which "Ganozae" transliterates the Hebrew phrase for "the garden of Uzza" (cf. 2 Kings 21:18, 26); the Greek also names his successor Jeconiah (here and in v. 9) rather than Jehoiachin.
notes.36:17: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "young man," the Greek reads "Zedekiah," and likewise has "His sanctuary" (singular) together with plural verbs ("they had no mercy... they led away").
notes.36:20: The Greek reads "until the kingdom of the Medes," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Persia" (though the Greek refers to "the Persians" in vv. 22-23).
notes.36:23: The Greek puts "to all the kingdoms of the earth" in the dative as the addressees of Cyrus's decree, leaving "The Lord God of heaven has given to me" without an expressed direct object (whereas the Hebrew makes "all the kingdoms of the earth" the object of "has given").
